name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,841

clue.text: Slender girl shapely after remodelling but needing A&E

indicators.note: A room that has been remodelled has the same parts in a new arrangement, which is what happens to the letters.
What you need is what you have not got, so the letters named are the ones missing from the mixture.

blocks.note: the letters of SHAPELY once its A and its E have gone
A&E is the British hospital's accident and emergency department, and the two letters it is made of are the ones dropped

explanation.surface: A girl left shapely by a makeover, except that the makeover has gone badly enough to need casualty.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E lets the clue name two letters while still talking about hospitals. The fodder has to be cut before it is shuffled, which is the order most solvers try last.
explanation.definitionFit: A sylph was an air spirit before it was a compliment, and it now means a slender, light-footed girl.

clue.text: Magnus Pym, a stereotype keeping control in Le Carré?

indicators.note: What a sentence keeps it holds inside itself, so the letters are sitting unbroken in the words as written.

blocks.note: the run starts on the last letter of Magnus: magnuS PYM A STEReotype

explanation.surface: A question about whether le Carré's Magnus Pym is a stock character who keeps his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Magnus Pym is the hero of le Carré's A Perfect Spy, so his name is doing double duty as scenery and as letters. 'Control' is capitalised in the Smiley novels and lower case here.
explanation.definitionFit: In le Carré the chief who runs the agents is called Control, so 'control' names the man in charge of spies rather than composure.

clue.text: Couple enjoy collecting new silver separately

indicators.note: A word that collects things gathers them inside itself, so the pieces named go within it.
The two pieces are not gathered together but at two different points, each slotting into its own gap.

blocks.note: to like something is to enjoy it
n is the standard short form of new
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum

explanation.surface: A couple who enjoy collecting antique silver, though each of them does the collecting alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' wants to be the pair doing the collecting and is the definition, in the old sense of a thing that joins. Ag is the chemist's symbol, not a shortening of the English word.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple is not only a pair but the thing that couples — a link or bond — and a linkage is exactly such a joining.

clue.text: Introductory line that chap will love

blocks.note: the pronoun that stands for the chap in question
'he will' contracts to he'll, and the contraction is where the two Ls come from
love is nil on a tennis scoreboard, written as the round letter

explanation.surface: An opening line that some chap is going to be delighted to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first three words aloud and the contraction does the work that no single word in the clue could. 'Love' for O is the tennis score, thought to come from the French l'oeuf, the egg-shaped nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello is the word you open with on meeting someone, so 'introductory line' describes the whole of its job.

clue.text: Rather inflexible suits returned by swimmer

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so those letters are read in the opposite direction.

blocks.note: a garment that suits you fits, and FITS sent back gives these four letters
the crossword's standard swimmer

explanation.surface: A swimmer posting some unyielding suits back to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suits' is a verb here — what fits you suits you — and that verb is the one that turns round. The two pieces meet at a doubled F, which is where the eye slides over the join.
explanation.definitionFit: The -ish ending waters an adjective down, so something stiffish is only rather stiff, which is to say rather inflexible.

clue.text: Honest fellow with spots on nose taking portrait back?

indicators.note: In a down entry one thing on another sits above it, so the first word's letters are written first.
To take something in is to admit it inside, so the letters named go within what has already been built.
Sent back, a word is read from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: to spot a thing is to sight it
hooter is British slang for a nose
a portrait is a piece of art, and ART arrives written backwards

explanation.surface: An honest man with a spotty nose returning the portrait somebody painted of him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' is the verb 'sights' and 'nose' is the slang hooter, so the blemishes never existed. ART for 'portrait' is a definition by example, which is what the question mark owns up to.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight shooter deals plainly and says what he means, the American idiom for an honest dealer.

clue.text: Fine cycling legend beyond description

indicators.note: Letters that cycle all move round one place in step, the front one coming round to the back.

blocks.note: the four letters of FINE with the first sent round to the end
a legend is a fable, a story told and retold

explanation.surface: A great cycling legend whose achievements are past describing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hands you a Tour de France hero, and both halves of that phrase are wrenched: 'cycling' turns into an instruction and 'legend' into a story rather than the rider who made it.
explanation.definitionFit: What is ineffable cannot be put into words at all, which is 'beyond description' in plain English.

clue.text: Set of instructions to make Chinese Disney film incomplete

indicators.note: Something left incomplete stops short of its end, so the final letter never arrives.

blocks.note: a recipe for a cake is a recipe to make a cake, so 'for' does the same work
Mulan, Disney's animation of the Chinese warrior legend, one letter short

explanation.surface: Instructions for making a Chinese Disney film that was never finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue needs nothing of the film but its title, which is why 'Chinese' and 'Disney' are there — between them they pin down one name. The definition is quiet work too: a formula is a set of steps before it is any chemistry.
explanation.definitionFit: A formula is the fixed sequence of steps for making something, in a kitchen as much as in a laboratory.

clue.text: Can it copy fashion?

blocks.note: 'can it' is a snapped order to be quiet, and so is 'sh'
to ape someone is to copy them

explanation.surface: A question about whether something is capable of imitating the latest fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can it' is the order to shut up rather than a question about ability, and it is the only way the first two letters arrive. The definition is the verb 'fashion', not the clothes the surface is thinking of.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion a thing is to shape it — the verb behind 'fashioned from clay' — and the two words swap freely.

clue.text: Orchestra playing Elgar holds back in symphony, mostly

indicators.note: Anything at play is loose and moving about, so those letters settle in an order of their own.
What a word holds it keeps inside itself, so the letter named goes within.

blocks.note: a band is an orchestra, and it opens after its first letter to take something in
the letter at the back of the word symphony
the composer's five letters in a new order

explanation.surface: An orchestra playing Elgar and holding back through most of the symphony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds back' reads as one phrase, musicians restraining themselves, and it is two separate instructions. The comma before 'mostly' is the only sign that the definition is standing alone at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: By and large means on the whole, allowing for the odd exception, which is what 'mostly' says.

clue.text: Study woodwind instrument's sound

indicators.note: A thing's sound is what reaches the ear, so the word is to be judged by ear and not by spelling.

blocks.note: the reed is the strip of cane an oboe or clarinet speaks through, and in an orchestra the reeds are those instruments themselves

explanation.surface: Studying the sound a woodwind instrument makes.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is about listening from beginning to end, which makes the homophone marker almost invisible: 'sound' looks like the thing being studied.
explanation.definitionFit: To read a subject is to study it, the sense in 'reading history at Oxford'.

clue.text: Motorway blocked by a vehicle dealing with bent tubes

indicators.note: A road blocked by something has it sitting in the middle of it, stopping the way through.

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, and its 1 doubles as the Roman numeral I
a car, both words taken straight
a report dealing with the weather is a report on the weather

explanation.surface: A motorway blocked by a car carrying badly bent piping.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is traffic and the definition is pasta, which is the whole of the misdirection. The number in a motorway's name is a common source of letters — 1 for I, 5 for V, 50 for L.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaroni is pasta made in short curved tubes, so 'bent tubes' is a description of what comes out of the packet.

clue.text: University on Florida island benefitting from fortune

indicators.note: In an across entry one thing sitting on another comes after it, so the university's letter is placed second.

blocks.note: FL is the two-letter postal abbreviation for Florida
u is the standard short form of university
a key is a low island or reef, as in the Florida Keys

explanation.surface: A university on an island off Florida that has come into money.
explanation.walkthrough: Florida supplies both halves of the picture, the state's abbreviation and the keys off its southern tip, while 'island' keeps the second one general. The adjective is more often spelt fluky, and both spellings are allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A flukey win comes off by luck rather than skill, so whoever gets one has benefitted from fortune.

clue.text: Act rated poorly Shakespeare's? Nothing in that

indicators.note: Anything done poorly is done badly, and letters handled badly come out in the wrong order.
'In that' points back at what has just been built and puts the letter named inside it.

blocks.note: the five letters of RATED in a new order
Shakespeare is the Bard, and the apostrophe-s comes along with him
nothing written as the round letter

explanation.surface: A badly reviewed act of a Shakespeare play, dismissed as having nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' at the front looks like a division of a play and is the verb. Shakespeare is the Bard in every crossword, but here it is his possessive that is wanted, apostrophe and all.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread the boards is to perform on a stage, the boards being the planks of the stage floor.

clue.text: European editor in the ascendancy taking on Channel 4 using logic

indicators.note: What is in the ascendancy is climbing, and in a down entry letters that climb are read from the bottom up.
To take something on is to take it in, so the letters that follow go inside what has been built.

blocks.note: e is the standard short form of European
ed is the usual short form of editor, as at the foot of a letters page
a duct is a channel carrying air or liquid
four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A European editor on the rise, taking on Channel 4.
explanation.walkthrough: Channel 4 is a British television station, and the clue writes it that way so it will be read as a name. What the wordplay wants is a plumbing channel and a Roman four.
explanation.definitionFit: Deductive reasoning drives from premises to a conclusion that has to follow, which is what 'using logic' names.

clue.text: Finish, say that Negrete demonstrated partly doing a flip

indicators.note: Only part of the words is wanted, and that part is a run of letters lying inside them.
A flip turns a thing head over heels, so the run of letters is taken from its far end back.

blocks.note: reading backwards from the d of 'demonstrated', through Negrete, to the last letter of 'that'

explanation.surface: A finishing move that a gymnast called Negrete half demonstrated while doing a flip.
explanation.walkthrough: Finish is a brand of dishwasher tablet, and 'say' is quietly flagging a definition by example rather than the end of a routine. A name you do not recognise in a clue is usually there to be read letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Finish is a brand of dishwasher detergent, so 'Finish, say' offers one example of the thing instead of defining it.

clue.text: Metro, sirens and riots in part of Paris

indicators.note: In a riot everything is thrown out of place, and letters thrown out of place come back in none of their original order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Sirens wailing through the Métro as riots break out across a Paris neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything in the surface belongs in Paris, so no word stands out as fodder. 'And' is part of the mixture rather than a joiner, which is the commonest place for a long anagram to go astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris is divided into twenty numbered arrondissements, so the word names one administrative district of the city.

clue.text: Yellow mosquito, for instance, that flies round and round

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun: 'that flies round and round' leans on the nouns in front of it, and the answer is the word for a thing which does it.

blocks.note: or is the heraldic name for gold or yellow on a coat of arms
a mosquito is one example of a biter

explanation.surface: A yellow mosquito of the sort that circles your head all night.
explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry supplies OR for yellow, one of the two metals a coat of arms may be painted in. 'For instance' is admitting that the mosquito is only an example of what the wordplay wants.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbiter is the craft that circles a planet instead of landing on it, so going round and round is all it does.

clue.text: Chase group inside 19 partying with drugs

blocks.note: the group of letters at the centre of HENGE, the answer to 19 down
a rave is a night of hard partying, drugs and all

explanation.surface: A pursuing group caught up inside a party where the drugs are going round.
explanation.walkthrough: The 19 is a cross-reference, so that entry has to be solved first, and what is wanted is the letters at its centre rather than the word itself. 'Chase' is a metalworker's verb here, nothing to do with pursuit.
explanation.definitionFit: To chase silver is to cut a pattern into its surface, which is the engraver's work under another name.

clue.text: Particularly afraid of supernatural creature in photo

indicators.note: 'In' puts what is named before it inside what comes after.

blocks.note: a pic is a photo, the everyday shortening
a hob is a goblin or house sprite of English folklore, the hob of hobgoblin

explanation.surface: Somebody badly frightened by the goblin that has turned up in a photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: A hob is the sprite behind 'hobgoblin'; in a modern British kitchen the same word means the cooker top, which is the sense the clue steers you away from. 'Particularly afraid' asks for the clinical adjective, not a merely frightened one.
explanation.definitionFit: To be phobic is to have a phobia, a fear out of all proportion to its object, so it is being afraid in one particular way.

clue.text: Ancient earthwork has hedgerow in the middle with bird laying eggs on it

indicators.note: What is wanted is the pair of letters at the very centre of the word, not the word itself.
In a down entry whatever sits on something is above it, so the bird's letters are written first.

blocks.note: the bird kept for the eggs we eat
the two letters at the centre of the eight-letter HEDGEROW

explanation.surface: An ancient earthwork with a hedgerow across its centre and a hen nesting on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' is there only to join, which is a hint that everything after it is wordplay. The word was worked backwards out of Stonehenge, and it properly names the bank and ditch rather than the stones.
explanation.definitionFit: A henge is the prehistoric circular bank and ditch enclosing a sacred site, earth heaped up by hand and so an ancient earthwork.

clue.text: Park warden trailing round yard where fruit trees grow

indicators.note: Something trailing another comes along behind it, so the warden's letters follow the round one.

blocks.note: the letter shaped like a ring
a ranger is the warden who patrols a park or forest
y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A park warden doing his rounds behind the yard where the fruit trees are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' is a letter and not a patrol, which is the one place where surface and wordplay part company. Y for yard is the builder's abbreviation, the one printed along a tape measure.
explanation.definitionFit: An orangery is the tall glasshouse a country house grew its oranges and lemons in, built so fruit trees could survive an English winter.

clue.text: Cold dry sandwiches unpleasant to smell and taste

indicators.note: To sandwich a thing is to shut it between two others, so the letter named goes inside.

blocks.note: arid land is dry land
c is the letter on the cold tap and in a weather forecast

explanation.surface: Cold dry sandwiches that are as bad to smell as they are to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' is a verb, which is the whole trick: the surface offers food while the clue is issuing an instruction. The definition is a single adjective spread over five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrid smoke catches at the nose and throat, and the same word covers a harsh bitter taste.

clue.text: Soldiers with egg on uniform

definitions.note: A unit is one body of soldiers, so the plural definition answers a singular noun: the setter is naming the men rather than the formation they make up.

indicators.note: In an across entry whatever sits on something comes after it, so the egg follows the letter taken from uniform.

blocks.note: uniform is the name for U in the NATO radio alphabet
a nit is the egg a louse leaves in the hair

explanation.surface: Soldiers on parade with a smear of egg on the uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: Both wordplay words hide inside the army picture: 'uniform' is the radio alphabet's name for a letter and 'egg' is the louse's. A nit is the egg rather than the insect, which is what a nit comb is for.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is the body of soldiers a battalion or platoon is made of, so naming the soldiers names it.

clue.text: Put underground cafes all over the place as meeting points

indicators.note: Things all over the place are in no order at all, so the letters land wherever they like.

blocks.note: to inter a body is to put it underground
the five letters of CAFES rearranged

explanation.surface: Underground cafes dotted all over the city and used as places to meet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put underground' is the burial verb, a long way from the coffee shops the rest of the surface is describing. The anagram covers only half the answer, which is why the fodder looks too short to be one.
explanation.definitionFit: An interface is the surface where two systems touch and pass things between them, so it is the point at which they meet.

clue.text: Call to approve two presents over the phone

indicators.note: Down a telephone line you get the sound of the words and none of their spelling.

blocks.note: a person present answers 'here' when the register is called, and the clue asks for two of them

explanation.surface: A phone call giving the go-ahead for a pair of gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presents' is the register-taking sense, the word you answer with when your name is read out, and the gifts are a decoy. Say it twice and the telephone does the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Hear, hear is the shout of agreement from the benches of the Commons, a call made to show approval of what has just been said.

clue.text: Mark from lash on deckhand's back remained

indicators.note: In an across entry one thing on another follows it, so the mark is written second.
The back of a word is its final letter, the one at the end of the line.

blocks.note: the last letter of DECKHAND
a welt is the raised ridge a lash leaves on skin

explanation.surface: The lash mark on a deckhand's back that has stayed there.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is so complete — a flogging aboard ship — that 'back' hardly looks like an instruction at all. 'Dwelt' is the older sense of dwell: to stay put rather than to live somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell is to stay or remain, and the past tense of the definition is matched by the past tense of the answer.
